templates.title: Weekly model downloads under a stated counting rule
templates.subtopic: deduplication to a daily grain, semi-joins, date-ranged exclusions, weekly rollups

sections.scenario: A model hub shows a download count on every model page. A model is a git repository of many files, and a single "download" by a library fetches several of them, so a count of file requests would mean nothing. This exercise publishes a counting rule instead (this exercise's rule; check current docs for any real hub's): for each library, a few designated files stand for "the model was downloaded"; a client counts at most once per model per UTC day; and clients on a published mirror list (caches that re-serve models to many users) are excluded while they are listed. You are writing the weekly report behind the per-model download chart for the two weeks from {{first_day}} to {{last_day}}.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns week_start, model_id, downloads, distinct_clients: one row per week and model with at least one counted download, ordered by week_start, model_id. A request counts when all of these hold: its path is one of the designated files for the model's library in counted_files (exact match); its http_status is below 400; and its client is not excluded that day. A client in mirror_clients is excluded on every UTC day d with listed_from <= d and (listed_until is NULL or d < listed_until). downloads is the number of distinct (client, UTC day) pairs with a counted request for the model in that week; distinct_clients is the number of distinct clients among them. week_start is the Monday (UTC) of the request's week, as a date. {{files_rule}} {{mirror_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Days and weeks are UTC: a request at 23:59:59 and one at 00:00:00 the next day are two days. The sample has {{requests}} file requests; a busy hub logs billions of file requests per day.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical models, libraries, designated files, clients and volumes. client_id is an anonymous client key the log already provides; nothing in this report identifies a person. Real counting rules differ and change; this one is fixed for the exercise.
sections.criteria: Designated files matched exactly per library; statuses below 400 only; mirrors excluded on listed days with an inclusive start and exclusive end; one download per (client, model, UTC day) before rolling up to weeks; correct Monday week starts; distinct_clients separate from downloads; deterministic order; can discuss restatement and scale.

clarifications.q: A client fetches the designated file three times on one day. How many downloads is that?
clarifications.a: One. A client counts at most once per model per UTC day.

clarifications.q: Does a 304 Not Modified count?
clarifications.a: Yes. Any status below 400 counts; 403, 404 and 500 do not.

clarifications.q: Is onnx/config.json the same as config.json?
clarifications.a: No. Paths match exactly.

clarifications.q: Is listed_until inclusive?
clarifications.a: No. A mirror is excluded from listed_from up to the day before listed_until; on listed_until itself it counts again.

clarifications.q: Which day does a week start on?
clarifications.a: Monday, UTC, so date_trunc('week', …) works as is.

clarifications.q: Should weeks with no downloads appear?
clarifications.a: No. Only (week, model) pairs with at least one counted download.

hints: Reduce the log to the grain of the rule first: one row per (model, client, UTC day) that has a counted request. SELECT DISTINCT does it.
The designated files depend on the model's library, so join file_requests to models and then to counted_files on both library and path.
The mirror exclusion depends on the day, so it is a NOT EXISTS with the date range inside it, not a plain anti-join on client_id.
followups: A model's library is changed in its card. Which days' counts change if you recompute, and how would you keep published counts stable?
The mirror list is updated after a week was published. How do you restate the affected weeks, and what do you show model owners?
At billions of file requests a day, design the daily pipeline: what do you keep (raw requests, the daily (model, client) set, the counts), for how long, and why?
A model owner says their count is too low because many users download from one corporate proxy. What does the rule do with that, and what would you change, if anything?

rules.ask: A client fetches the designated file ten times in one day. What does your count give, and what does the rule say?
A mirror was listed only for the second half of the period. Which of its requests should still count, and where does your query decide that?
Does onnx/config.json match your condition? Should it?
Where does a request at Sunday 23:59:59 UTC go, and one a second later?
What exactly is the grain of your DISTINCT, and what changes if the day is left out of it?

templates.title: Gated repositories: hours from access request to decision
templates.subtopic: first and latest event per key, PERCENTILE_CONT, point-in-time cutoffs

sections.scenario: On a model hub, a repository may require users to accept conditions or request access before they can download its files. Some gated repos approve requests automatically; on others a maintainer reviews each request. The hub wants to show maintainers how long requesters wait, and to see which repos have a backlog. Automatic approvals take seconds and would drag a combined median towards zero, so auto-approving repos are reported apart. You are writing the report as of {{as_of}}.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns repo_id, approval_mode, requests, accepted, rejected, pending, median_hours_to_decision: one row per gated repo with at least one request before the cutoff, ordered by approval_mode, repo_id (so the auto repos come first, apart from the manual ones). Only requests and decisions strictly before {{as_of}} exist for this report. For each request, the wait is from requested_at to its first decision; its outcome is its latest decision (ties on decided_at broken by decision_id); a request with no decision is pending. accepted, rejected and pending count requests by outcome. median_hours_to_decision is PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) of the waits of decided requests, in hours, rounded to 2 decimal places; it is NULL for auto repos and for a repo with no decided request. {{decision_rule}} {{cutoff_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Pending requests are counted, never treated as a wait of zero or as waiting until the cutoff. The sample has {{requests}} requests.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical repos, users and timings; gating is described generally (a repo may require accepting conditions before access) and this report says nothing about any licence. The approval modes are this exercise's simplification.
sections.criteria: Cutoff applied to both requests and decisions, strictly; wait to the first decision and outcome from the latest with a deterministic tie-break; pending requests counted and kept out of the median; median NULL for auto repos and for repos without decisions; PERCENTILE_CONT rounded to 2 places; deterministic order; can discuss reporting open requests honestly.

clarifications.q: A request was rejected and later accepted. When did its wait end?
clarifications.a: At the first decision. The reversal changes the outcome to accepted, not the wait.

clarifications.q: Do pending requests enter the median?
clarifications.a: No. They are counted in pending only. (Follow-up 2 asks what that hides.)

clarifications.q: Why is the median NULL for auto repos?
clarifications.a: Their decisions are automatic; a median of seconds would only blur the manual repos' figure. The counts are still reported.

clarifications.q: A decision is stamped exactly at the cutoff. Does it count?
clarifications.a: No. Only events strictly before the cutoff exist for this report.

clarifications.q: Which percentile?
clarifications.a: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5): the average of the two middle values when the count is even.

hints: Filter both tables to the cutoff first, so everything after it simply does not exist.
Number each request's decisions twice with ROW_NUMBER(): ascending for the first, descending for the latest. Join both back to the requests with LEFT JOINs so pending requests survive.
PERCENTILE_CONT ignores NULLs, so a NULL wait for a pending request is excluded automatically; a CASE on approval_mode makes the auto repos' median NULL.
followups: A maintainer asks for "median wait including the ones still waiting". How would you report waiting requests honestly: their age so far, a survival curve, or something else?
Requests can be withdrawn by the requester. How do you add that state, and which counts change?
The decision log is append-only, but one day of decisions was replayed twice by a buggy job. How does your query behave, and what constraint or step would protect it?
The hub wants this per repo per week, recomputed daily. Which numbers can change after a week ends, and how do you store the report so the changes are visible?

rules.ask: You took the latest decision. Which question does that answer, the outcome or the wait? What should the other one use?
What happens to a request that has no decision yet? Where does it appear in your result?
A few requests waited a week. What does that do to the mean, and why does the report use the median?
The report is as of a fixed cutoff. What does your query return if it is rerun next month?
A decision is stamped exactly at the cutoff. Is it in your report, and should it be?

templates.title: Every derivative of a base model, from declared base-model metadata
templates.subtopic: transitive closure, diamonds, cycle guards, dirty user-supplied links

sections.scenario: On a model hub, a model card can declare the model's base model and how the model relates to it: fine-tuned from it, an adapter on it, a quantised copy of it, or a merge of several models. Derivatives have derivatives of their own, so a popular base model sits at the root of a large family tree. The hub wants a "derivatives" panel on each model page: how many models descend from it at any depth, by kind. The declarations are user content and are not checked: they can name repos that are not on the hub, a model can name itself, and in the hardest case they can loop. {{data_rule}}
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns model_id, direct_derivatives, descendants, finetunes, adapters, quantized, merges: one row for every model in models that has at least one descendant, ordered by descendants descending, then model_id. model_bases holds one row per declaration: model_id declares base_model_id as a base. A model's descendants are the distinct models other than itself reachable by following declarations from base to derivative, at any depth. direct_derivatives is the number of distinct other models that declare it directly. finetunes, adapters, quantized and merges count its descendants by the descendant's own base_relation ('finetune', 'adapter', 'quantized', 'merge').
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (a recursive CTE is expected). A model is never its own descendant, and a descendant reachable by several paths counts once. Declared bases that are not in models get no row. The query must terminate on any input. The sample has {{models}} models and {{links}} declarations.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical model ids and relations. Every model with a declared base has a base_relation; models without one are originals. The relation values follow the kind of metadata model cards can carry, simplified for the exercise.
sections.criteria: Correct transitive closure with distinct descendants; self-declarations and self-pairs excluded; terminates on cycles; counts by the descendant's own relation; direct derivatives counted separately; only models in models reported; deterministic order; can discuss storing and maintaining the closure.

clarifications.q: A merge declares two bases that both descend from the same original. How many times does the merge count for the original?
clarifications.a: Once. Descendants are distinct models.

clarifications.q: Which relation decides the column?
clarifications.a: The descendant's own base_relation. A quantised copy of a fine-tune counts under quantized for every ancestor.

clarifications.q: A model declares itself as its base.
clarifications.a: Ignore that declaration; it does not make the model its own derivative.

clarifications.q: What if declarations form a loop?
clarifications.a: Every model on the loop reaches the others, so they are each other's descendants, but none is its own.

clarifications.q: What about a declared base that is not in models?
clarifications.a: It has no row. Its derivatives are still models and can be descendants of other models.

hints: Build the closure as pairs (ancestor, descendant): start from every declaration, then extend each pair by one more declaration.

UNION (not UNION ALL) in a recursive CTE discards pairs already produced, which both removes duplicate paths and stops cycles. Alternatively carry a path array and stop when the next model is already on it.
Drop self-declarations up front, and drop ancestor = descendant pairs before counting.
followups: Your closure has one row per (ancestor, descendant). For a base model with 50 000 descendants, how big is the closure across the whole hub, and when would you store it instead of computing it?
A card edit changes one model's declared base. Which rows of a stored closure change, and how would you update them incrementally?
The panel should also show the depth of the nearest path to each descendant. What changes in the recursion, and what does a cycle do to it?
How would you flag declarations that are probably wrong (cycles, bases newer than their derivatives), and where would you show that?

rules.ask: Two paths lead to the same merge. What does UNION ALL do with it, and what happens if declarations loop?
You carry a path array. How long can a path get, and what does the array cost compared with deduplicating pairs?
You stop at a fixed depth. How do you know it is deep enough, and what does the query return for a chain one level deeper?
A declared base is not on the hub. Does your query still reach its derivatives from their other ancestors?
Besides a model declaring itself, how else could a model reach itself, and where does your query exclude that?

templates.title: Dataset viewer paging across converted row shards
templates.subtopic: locating global offsets in ordered chunks

sections.scenario: A dataset hub shows the first rows of every dataset in a viewer and lets people page through all of it. To make that possible, each pushed dataset is converted into ordered shards of rows (a large dataset has thousands). The viewer asks for pages by global row number, "rows 1 200 000 to 1 200 099", and the server must say which shards to read and where in them. Conversion can still be running when someone opens the viewer. {{data_rule}}
sections.problem: Implement locate_pages(shard_rows, requests). shard_rows[i] is the number of rows in shard i, in dataset order; global rows are numbered from 0 through the shards in that order. Each request is (offset, length): the rows offset … offset + length − 1. For each request return a list of segments (shard_index, first_row_in_shard, n_rows) that covers those rows in order, with no segment of 0 rows (an empty shard never appears). A page that runs past the last row is cut at the end, and a page that starts at or after the end is []. If any shard is None (not converted yet), the rows of that shard and of every shard after it have unknown positions: a request that needs any row at or beyond the first None shard returns None instead of a list.
sections.constraints: Up to 30 000 shards and 80 000 requests; a shard holds up to 10 000 rows, so a dataset can have hundreds of millions of rows. offset ≥ 0 and length ≥ 1. Expected: O(s + q log s + output). Walking the shards from the first for every request is too slow, and expanding rows into a list does not fit in memory.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical shard sizes and requests; the conversion and the viewer are this exercise's model, not a description of any hub's service. Shard sizes are known exactly once a shard is converted.
sections.criteria: Prefix starts over non-empty shards and a binary search per request; correct segments across boundaries with no empty segment; [] past the end and cutting at the end; None for any row at or beyond the first unconverted shard while the converted prefix is still served; O(s + q log s + output); can discuss incremental conversion and filtered paging.

clarifications.q: A page ends exactly at the end of a shard. Is there a segment for the next shard?
clarifications.a: No. Every segment has at least one row.

clarifications.q: What do I return for a page that starts past the end?
clarifications.a: An empty list [], if every shard is converted.

clarifications.q: Shards 0–4 are converted, 5 is not, 6 is. Can I serve rows from shard 6?
clarifications.a: No. Its position depends on shard 5's size, so any row at or beyond shard 5 is unknown and the request returns None.

clarifications.q: A page ends exactly at the last converted row, before a None shard.
clarifications.a: It is fully known: return its segments.

clarifications.q: Can a shard have 0 rows?
clarifications.a: Yes. It holds no rows and never appears in a segment.

hints: Precompute the global row number where each non-empty shard starts. That list is sorted.
bisect_right(starts, offset) − 1 is the shard holding row offset; from there, walk forward only as far as the page goes.
Decide None, cut and [] from the totals before locating anything.
followups: Shards are converted one at a time and appended. How do you keep the start list up to date without rebuilding it, and what if an earlier shard is reconverted with a different row count?
The viewer also filters rows (say, only rows whose label is 3). How does paging change when a page is "the next 100 matching rows"?
The service is stateless and runs on many machines. Where does the start list live, and how large is it for a dataset with a million shards?
A user jumps to the middle of a 2-billion-row dataset. Which reads does your design make, and how would you make the first page fast?

rules.ask: You walk the shards for every request. With 30 000 shards and 80 000 requests, how many steps is that, and how do you avoid it?
The dataset has hundreds of millions of rows. How much memory does a per-row list take?
Which bisect variant did you use, and what does it return for an offset that is exactly the first row of a shard?
Shard 5 is not converted but shard 6 is. Why can't you serve shard 6, and what would you need to know to do so?

templates.title: Reclaimable large-file storage after branches and tags are deleted
templates.subtopic: mark phase of mark-and-sweep over a commit DAG, iterative DFS

sections.scenario: Model and dataset repositories on a hub are git repositories in which large files (weights, shards) are stored as content-addressed objects outside the git history, referenced by small pointer files. Deleting a file in a new commit does not free its bytes, because history still references it; bytes are freed only when no remaining branch or tag can reach any commit that references the object. A repository owner deletes some branches and tags and asks how much storage that frees. You are writing the estimate (this exercise's retention rule; check current docs for any real service's). {{history_rule}}
sections.problem: Implement reclaimable(commits, refs, deleted, store, pinned). Each commit is (commit_id, parent_ids, oids), where oids are the large-file objects that commit wrote. refs maps every branch and tag name to a commit id, before deletion; deleted lists the ref names being deleted (a name that is not in refs changes nothing). store maps every object the repository holds to its size in bytes. An object is kept if it is in pinned, or if some commit reachable from a remaining ref (following parent_ids at any depth) wrote it. A parent id or ref that names a commit not in commits leads nowhere. Return (count, bytes) for the objects in store that are not kept. An object that a commit names but store does not hold is ignored.
sections.constraints: Up to 150 000 commits, about 150 000 objects and 1 000 refs; history chains can be 150 000 commits deep, so a recursive walk overflows Python's stack. Expected: O(C + P + F) for C commits, P parent links and F object references. A reachability search per object (or per ref, without sharing what was already visited) is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical commits, objects and sizes. The retention rule is this exercise's simplification: a real service may keep objects longer (grace periods, open pull requests, other repositories sharing the store), which is what pinned stands for.
sections.criteria: One iterative traversal from the remaining refs with a shared visited set; objects kept if any reachable commit wrote them, or pinned; deleted names that do not exist ignored; unknown commit ids skipped; orphan uploads reclaimable, unknown objects ignored; O(C + P + F); can discuss forks sharing a store, attribution and safe sweeping.

clarifications.q: A file is deleted in a later commit on a remaining branch. Is its object freed?
clarifications.a: No. The earlier commit that wrote it is still in the branch's history.

clarifications.q: Do I need to rebuild the full file tree of each commit?
clarifications.a: No. An object is kept if any reachable commit wrote it; that is all the rule needs.

clarifications.q: A branch and a tag point at the same commit, and only the branch is deleted.
clarifications.a: The tag keeps that commit and its history.

clarifications.q: An object was uploaded but no commit ever referenced it.
clarifications.a: It is not kept, so it is reclaimable.

clarifications.q: The same object was written on two branches.
clarifications.a: It is kept as long as either branch remains.

hints: This is the mark phase of mark-and-sweep: mark every commit reachable from the remaining refs once, collect the objects they wrote, then sweep the store.
Use an explicit stack and a seen set shared by all refs, so every commit is visited once whatever the number of refs.
Skip ids you do not know instead of failing on them.
followups: Forks share one object store. How would you compute what deleting a fork frees, and why does pinned turn into a reference count?
The owner wants to see which deleted branch is responsible for most of the freed bytes. Define that carefully: what about bytes only freed when two branches are both deleted?
On a store with billions of objects, the mark phase cannot be done in one process. How would you split it, and how do you stay safe against a push that lands during the sweep?
Why do real systems wait (a grace period) before deleting unreferenced objects, and what does that change in your estimate?

rules.ask: The history is a chain of 150 000 commits. What happens to your recursive walk, and how do you rewrite it?
You search the history once per object. With 150 000 objects and 150 000 commits, how much work is that?
Do you need each commit's full file tree to decide whether an object is kept? What does that cost in memory?
Is your visited set shared across refs? How many times is a commit on a shared trunk visited otherwise?

templates.title: Changed files between two revisions of a hub repository
templates.subtopic: content-addressed directory trees, pruned recursive diff

sections.scenario: Models and datasets on a public hub live in git-style repositories. A commit points at a root tree. A tree lists names, and each name points at a file object or at another tree, by an id derived from the content. Two trees with the same id hold exactly the same files. A dataset repository can hold tens of thousands of files in nested directories, and most commits touch a handful of them. Several features need the list of files that changed between two commits: a "files changed" view, a job that decides which converted files are stale, and a notice to people who watch the repository. Flattening both revisions into full path lists for every request is too slow on large repositories, and many such diffs are requested every minute.
sections.problem: Implement diff_revisions(trees, commits, pairs). trees maps a tree id to its entries, {name: (mode, object_id)}, where mode is 'file', 'exec' (an executable file) or 'dir'. A 'dir' entry's object_id is another tree id in trees. commits maps a commit id to its root tree id. For each (old, new) in pairs, return the list of changed file paths as (path, status) tuples, sorted by path as a plain string. A path is the names from the root joined by /. Status 'A' means the file exists only in new, 'D' only in old, and 'M' in both with a different object id or a different mode. Directories are never listed themselves: an added or deleted directory lists every file below it. A file replaced by a directory of the same name is a 'D' for the file and an 'A' for every file in the new directory, and the reverse for a directory replaced by a file. There is no rename detection: a moved file is a 'D' and an 'A'. If either commit id is not in commits, that pair's entry is None. If both sides are the same commit, the entry is []. Return one entry per pair, in the order of pairs. {{tree_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 100 000 files, 3 000 commits and 1 000 pairs per call. Trees are never empty and are at most 12 levels deep. Names contain no /. The work for one pair should grow with the number of changed files times the depth of the tree, not with the size of the repository. Flattening both revisions for every pair is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Repository contents, ids and sizes are hypothetical. Ids are opaque strings: two equal tree ids mean identical subtrees, but you cannot read anything else from an id. Large files stored outside the repository appear here as ordinary file objects (their pointers), so a change to a large file is a change of object id like any other. Symbolic links and submodules do not appear.
sections.criteria: Correct statuses including mode-only changes; files listed below added and deleted directories; file-to-directory and directory-to-file replacements; None for unknown commits and [] for the same commit; results sorted by the whole path string; a simultaneous walk that never opens subtrees with equal ids; a clear complexity argument (changed files × depth × entries per changed tree) against O(files) per pair; sensible answers on caching, rename detection and very wide directories.

clarifications.q: Is a directory that was added listed as one entry?
clarifications.a: No. Only files are listed, so an added directory lists every file under it, recursively.

clarifications.q: A file's content is the same but it became executable. Is that a change?
clarifications.a: Yes, status 'M': the mode is part of the entry.

clarifications.q: Should I detect renames?
clarifications.a: No. A moved file is a 'D' at the old path and an 'A' at the new one, even when the object id is the same.

clarifications.q: How are the results sorted?
clarifications.a: By the whole path string, as Python's sorted orders strings. That is not always the order a recursive walk visits them: 'onnx-int8/…' sorts before 'onnx.json', which sorts before 'onnx/…'.

clarifications.q: What if a pair names a commit that does not exist?
clarifications.a: That pair's entry is None. The other pairs are answered normally.

clarifications.q: Can old be newer than new?
clarifications.a: Yes. The diff is just from the old side to the new side, so additions and deletions swap.

hints: If the two root tree ids are equal, nothing differs. The same is true for any pair of subtrees: equal ids mean you never have to open them.

Walk the two trees together, name by name. Recurse only where both sides are directories with different ids. Where one side is missing, or a file meets a directory, list all the files below the directory that is there.
Collect the changes in a list and sort once at the end, rather than trying to emit them in order during the walk.
followups: The same diff is requested many times, for example by every visitor of a popular "files changed" page. What would you cache, keyed by what, and why is that cache never stale?
Users ask for rename detection: a deleted path and an added path with the same object id. How would you add it, and what do you do when one object id is deleted at one path and added at three?

A repository has one directory with 200 000 files in it, and a commit changes one of them. Your diff still reads both 200 000-entry trees. What changes to the tree layout or the comparison would avoid that?
A job needs the changed paths for every commit pushed to the hub, across all repositories, and passes them to search indexing and the dataset viewer. Where does this diff run, and what does it emit?

rules.ask: How many paths do you build per pair on a 64 000-file repository, and how many pairs arrive per minute? What does that cost?
You skip subtrees with equal ids. What property of the ids makes that safe, and what would break if ids were assigned by counter instead of from content?
What is your cache key, and can a cached diff ever become wrong when new commits are pushed?
Trees can be 12 levels deep here. What happens to your recursion on a pathological repository 5 000 levels deep, and how would you make it iterative?
Your rename detection pairs a deleted path with an added one by object id. Two empty files share one id. What does your code report?

templates.title: Test rows that overlap the train split
templates.subtopic: n-gram sets, text normalisation, train–test overlap per dataset

sections.scenario: Dataset repositories on a public hub often ship a train split and a test split. When a test row repeats a passage from the train split, scores measured on that test split look better than they should. A maintainer wants a check that runs whenever a dataset revision is pushed: for every test row, does it share a run of n consecutive words with any train row of the same dataset? This exercise's rule uses n = {{n}}. A shared run that long is unlikely to be chance, and short enough to catch passages copied with small changes around them.
sections.problem: Implement split_overlap(datasets, n). datasets maps a dataset name to (train_rows, test_rows), two lists of strings. A row's words are found by lower-casing it and taking every maximal run of ASCII letters and digits; everything else separates words, so "Step-by-step!" is the three words step, by, step. An n-gram is n consecutive words of one row; rows are never joined, so no n-gram spans two rows. A test row overlaps if at least one of its n-grams is also an n-gram of a train row of the same dataset. For every dataset, return a list of (test_index, train_index) for the overlapping test rows, sorted by test_index, where train_index is the smallest index of a train row that shares at least one n-gram with that test row. Every dataset in the input appears in the output, with [] when no test row overlaps. A row with fewer than n words has no n-grams and never overlaps. {{text_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 20 datasets, 50 000 train rows and 10 000 test rows per dataset, and up to 300 words per row; 2 ≤ n ≤ 20. Something close to linear in the total number of words is expected. Comparing every test row with every train row is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Datasets, rows and sizes are hypothetical, and the text is ASCII. The check only reports overlaps; deciding what to do about them is the maintainer's choice. Exact n-gram matching after the normalisation above is the whole rule: no stemming, no fuzzy matching.
sections.criteria: Exact tokenisation as specified; no n-grams across rows; rows shorter than n never flagged; per-dataset matching with every dataset present in the output; the smallest train index, not the first found; a single dict from n-gram to smallest index, O(total words · n) to build and query; a clear comparison with the O(train × test) approach; credible answers on scale (hashing, sharding by n-gram, MinHash or suffix structures) and on false positives from boilerplate.

clarifications.q: Do rows from different datasets count?
clarifications.a: No. Only train rows of the same dataset.

clarifications.q: If a test row shares n-grams with several train rows, which index do I report?
clarifications.a: The smallest train row index among all of them, not the first one you happen to find while scanning the test row.

clarifications.q: Is punctuation part of a word?
clarifications.a: No. Words are runs of ASCII letters and digits after lower-casing, so "Hello," and "hello" are the same word, and an apostrophe or hyphen splits a word.

clarifications.q: Can an n-gram run from the end of one train row into the start of the next?
clarifications.a: No. Each row is a separate piece of text.

clarifications.q: What about a test row with fewer than n words?
clarifications.a: It has no n-grams, so it is never reported, even if it appears word for word inside a train row.

hints: Build one structure from the train split first, then answer each test row from it, instead of comparing pairs of rows.
A tuple of n words is hashable. A dict from tuple to the smallest train index answers "which train row, if any" in one lookup.
Insert into the dict only if the n-gram is not already there, and visit train rows in index order. Then the stored index is already the smallest.
followups: The train split is 400 GB of text and the dict no longer fits in memory. How would you run the same check, and what would you use instead of exact tuples?

A maintainer wants overlaps between a new dataset's test split and the train splits of 5 000 other datasets on the hub. What would you precompute, and how would you keep it current as those datasets are pushed?
Long numbers, licence headers and boilerplate like "the following is a conversation" create overlaps that are not leaks. How would you suppress them without hiding real ones?
How would you choose n, and what evidence would you show a maintainer that the number of flagged rows is meaningful?

rules.ask: How long is the joined train text, and how many substring searches do you run? What is the total cost?
You intersect a test row's n-grams with each train row's set. How many row pairs is that at 50 000 × 10 000?
Two different n-grams can hash to the same value. What does a collision do to your answer, and how would you confirm a hit?
You join words with a space to make a key. Could two different word lists ever produce the same key here? What about if words could contain spaces?
A Bloom filter can say "maybe present" for an n-gram that is not there. How do you get the smallest train index, and what is your false-positive rate at this size?

templates.title: Debug the repository activity digest
templates.subtopic: stable ids versus names, visibility at event time, UTC days, deletes and restores

sections.scenario: A public hub sends each user a daily digest of activity on public repositories: how many pushes each repository received on each day. Repositories are renamed, transferred between users and organisations, deleted and sometimes restored, and switched between private and public. Support has collected complaints about one function. Renamed models show no history from before the rename. A private model that an organisation took over shows up in the digest. A dataset that was deleted by mistake and restored lost all its earlier activity. Pushes made while a model was still private appear once it is made public. And people in some time zones see pushes on the wrong day. The function below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix activity_digest(events) so that it meets this specification. events is a list of dicts in the order the hub committed them. Every event has "type", "repo" (a stable repository id that never changes) and "ts" (an ISO 8601 timestamp with a UTC offset, such as "2026-10-13T20:30:00-05:00"). {{replay_rule}}

  1. create has "name" ("owner/name") and "private" (a bool). rename has "name", the new repository name without the owner. transfer has "owner", the new owner; the name and the visibility are unchanged. visibility has "private". delete and restore have nothing more. A restored repository comes back exactly as it was, with its name, owner, visibility and history.
  2. A push counts if the repository exists, is not deleted and is public at the moment of the push. Pushes the hub rejected because the repository was deleted are still in the log, and are ignored. Events for an id that was never created are ignored.
  3. A counted push belongs to the UTC calendar day of its timestamp.
  4. The digest reports a repository under its final "owner/name", after every event. A repository that is deleted or private at the end is left out entirely, with all its history.
  5. Output. {"YYYY-MM-DD": {"owner/name": pushes}}. Days and repositories with no counted pushes do not appear.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 200 000 events, processed in linear time.
sections.assumptions: Event shapes, names and volumes are hypothetical, and the visibility and digest rules are this exercise's rules (check current docs for how the hub actually behaves). The final names of repositories that exist at the end are unique. A deleted repository receives no events except rejected pushes and a restore.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its user-visible symptom; accumulates by stable repository id and names at the end; a transfer that changes only the owner; deletes that hide but do not erase, so restores keep history; visibility checked at push time and at the end; UTC days from offset timestamps; minimal, linear fixes; a regression check per bug.

clarifications.q: A repository was public, then made private. Are its earlier public pushes shown?
clarifications.a: No. A repository that is private at the end is left out entirely, so its name never appears.

clarifications.q: Does a transfer change visibility?
clarifications.a: No. A private repository transferred to an organisation stays private.

clarifications.q: Which name does a push made before a rename appear under?
clarifications.a: The final name. The digest is keyed by repository, and shows its name as it is now.

clarifications.q: Which day is "the day" of a push?
clarifications.a: The UTC date of the timestamp, after applying its offset. 2026-10-13T20:30:00-05:00 is on 2026-10-14.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Which value identifies a repository for its whole life? Key everything you accumulate by that, and look the name up once at the end.
Write out what the record looks like before and after a transfer of a private repository.
Visibility matters twice: at the moment of each push, and at the end.
What does a delete need to change, if a restore must bring everything back?
followups: The digest is computed for millions of users from billions of events. How would you compute it incrementally each day instead of replaying all history?
A repository is renamed after yesterday's digest was sent. Should yesterday's digest change? What do you store so that both answers are possible?
A user asks to be forgotten, and their repositories are deleted for good. How does that reach every derived table, including digests already computed?

Events arrive from several services, and a visibility event sometimes lands a few seconds after a push it should precede. What ordering guarantee do you need, and how would you handle the cases where you do not get it?

rules.ask: Your timestamps are converted to UTC. What does a user in UTC−08:00 expect to see as "yesterday", and how would you offer that without breaking the UTC totals?
You key by repository id now. If two repositories end with the same name, which one is shown, and how could that happen on a real hub?
Deleting no longer purges. When must data from a deleted repository actually be removed, and how would you do it?
You check visibility at the end. Show an event sequence where that check alone shows activity that was private when it happened.
Your transfer builds a new record. Which fields could it lose, and how do you make sure a new field added next year is not lost too?

templates.title: One event stream for hub repository changes
templates.subtopic: change events, ordering per key, fan-out to search, cards and notifications

sections.scenario: A public hub hosts about {{repos}} model, dataset and Spaces repositories and receives about {{pushes_per_day}} pushes a day. Besides pushes, repositories get tags and branches, renames, transfers between owners, visibility changes, gating changes and deletions. Today, {{consumers}} features each poll repositories or listen to their own ad-hoc hooks: search indexing, the parsed metadata from model and dataset cards, notifications to watchers, the dataset viewer and others. They disagree about what a repository is called and whether it is public, and a private repository has once appeared in search results for a few minutes after it was made private. You are asked to design one stream of repository events that every feature consumes, with changes visible to consumers within {{freshness}}.
sections.problem: Design the repository event stream and how it is fed and consumed. Cover where events come from and how a push becomes an event only once it is committed, the event schema (stable repository id, a per-repository sequence number, event types and payloads), ordering guarantees and the partition key, what a consumer does with each event type (in particular renames, transfers, visibility changes and deletions), how a new consumer builds its state from scratch, replay and retention, schema evolution, and how you would check that every consumer agrees with the repositories' real state.
sections.constraints: A repository that becomes private or is deleted must disappear from every public surface within {{freshness}}. Consumers are owned by different teams and fail independently. Events about one repository must be applied in order; events about different repositories need not be. A push can contain thousands of files, and its event must not carry their contents.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, freshness targets and the list of consumers are hypothetical. Repositories are git-based, and the hub already knows when a push is committed. You may use common open building blocks: a partitioned log, a stream processor, a key-value store, a search index and object storage.
sections.criteria: Events emitted only for committed changes; stable id and per-repository sequence numbers; partitioning that preserves per-repository order with a plan for hot repositories; a schema with versioning and pointers instead of file contents; privacy-sensitive events handled with priority or a re-read of current state, and measured against the {{freshness}} target; bootstrap from a snapshot plus the log; replay, retention and tombstones; consumer independence and lag monitoring; a reconciliation that proves public surfaces match the real state; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: What identifies a repository in events?
clarifications.a: A stable id assigned at creation. Names and owners change; the id never does.

clarifications.q: Does a push event list the changed files?
clarifications.a: You decide. Listing every changed path can be large. A pointer to the old and new commit lets a consumer compute the diff itself.

clarifications.q: Is "deleted" final?
clarifications.a: Not always: a repository can be restored within a period set by this exercise's rule. Consumers must handle both.

clarifications.q: Who is harmed by a late visibility change?
clarifications.a: The owner of a private repository, whose name, card or files may be shown publicly. That case matters more than any other latency.

clarifications.q: Can consumers call back into the hub for the current state?
clarifications.a: Yes, through an internal read API, but every consumer doing that on every event is what overloads the hub today.

hints: Partition by the stable repository id, and number events per repository. A consumer can then detect gaps and duplicates by itself.
Visibility changes and deletions are different from other events: think about whether they should be "facts to apply" or "triggers to re-read the current state".
A new consumer needs a starting state. A compacted snapshot of each repository's latest state plus the log from that point is a common answer.
followups: A consumer was down for six hours. How does it catch up, and what do public surfaces show for repositories that went private during those hours?
A repository is renamed, and its old name is taken by a new repository a minute later. Walk through what search, notifications and card metadata each do.
You add a new event type for gating changes. How do existing consumers that do not know it behave?
How would you prove, every day, that no private or deleted repository is visible on any public surface?
One organisation pushes 200 000 times in an hour from an automated job. What does that do to your partitions and to other repositories' freshness?

rules.ask: One very active repository lands on one partition. What happens to the other repositories on that partition, and what would you do about it?
Which consumers actually need exactly-once effects, and which are fine with at-least-once delivery plus idempotent writes keyed by sequence number?
Some consumers are outside your control and use webhooks. How do they get the same ordering and the same privacy guarantee?
You key something by name. What happens to it on a rename followed by a new repository taking the old name?
Your compacted topic keeps the latest state per repository. How does a consumer learn that a repository was deleted, and when is that tombstone itself removed?

incidents: A consumer's lag grows to 40 minutes after a deploy, while {{pushes_per_day}} pushes a day keep arriving, and a repository made private during that time still appears in that consumer's search results.
A bug in the producer emits two events with the same per-repository sequence number but different payloads for about 300 repositories.
A burst of renames and transfers from an organisation migrating 50 000 repositories makes notification volume spike and watchers receive notices under old names.

templates.title: Converting pushed datasets for the dataset viewer
templates.subtopic: per-revision conversion jobs, columnar shards, retries, stale-while-converting

sections.scenario: A public hub hosts about {{datasets}} dataset repositories. A dataset viewer lets anyone page through the rows of a dataset, filter them and see column statistics, without downloading anything. To make that fast, each pushed revision is converted into columnar shards with a fixed row-group size, and the viewer reads those. Datasets arrive in about {{formats}} formats (CSV, JSON lines, columnar files, image and audio folders, archives and others) and range from a few rows to {{max_size}}. The hub receives about {{pushes_per_day}} pushes to dataset repositories a day, sometimes several to the same dataset within minutes. Some conversions fail: malformed files, columns whose types change from file to file, or a dataset too large for the limits. You are designing the conversion pipeline and what the viewer shows while it works.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from a dataset push to rows in the viewer. Cover how a push becomes conversion work (and how several quick pushes to one dataset are handled), the unit of work (dataset, revision, configuration and split), job states, retries and the difference between a transient failure and a failure that will repeat, how converted shards are stored and addressed by revision, what the viewer shows for a revision that is not converted yet or failed, large datasets and partial conversion, schema inference and its errors, quotas so that one huge dataset cannot starve the others, and how you would know the pipeline is healthy.
sections.constraints: The viewer must never mix rows from two revisions. A failed conversion must tell the dataset's owner what went wrong in words they can act on. Re-running a job for the same revision must produce the same shards. Datasets may be gated or private, and their converted shards must be governed by the same access rules as the repository. Compute is shared, and cost matters.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, sizes, formats and limits are hypothetical, and partial-conversion and size limits are this exercise's rules (check current docs). The hub already publishes an event when a push to a repository is committed, with the old and new commit ids. A dataset's configurations and splits can be read from its files or its card.
sections.criteria: Conversion triggered by committed pushes with coalescing per dataset; a job key that includes the revision, immutable outputs and an atomic switch of the current pointer; a clear viewer state for converting, failed and partial revisions with no mixing of revisions; transient versus deterministic failures; fair scheduling and quotas for very large datasets; deterministic reruns; access control on converted shards equal to the repository's; useful health metrics (queue age, failure rate by cause, time from push to viewable); a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Must every revision be converted?
clarifications.a: No. Only what the viewer needs: usually the latest revision of the main branch. Converting every intermediate push is waste.

clarifications.q: What does the viewer show while a new revision converts?
clarifications.a: You decide, and justify it: the previous revision's rows clearly labelled, a progress state, or nothing.

clarifications.q: Are very large datasets converted completely?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, a dataset above a size limit is converted only up to the limit, and the viewer says so.

clarifications.q: Can a job fail forever?
clarifications.a: Yes, for example a malformed file. Retrying it every hour wastes compute; it should wait for a new push.

clarifications.q: Who can see converted rows of a gated dataset?
clarifications.a: The same people who can read the repository's files. Converted shards are a copy of the data, not public metadata.

hints: Make the job key (dataset, revision, config, split), and make each job's output immutable and addressed by that key. Then "which rows does the viewer show" becomes "which revision's pointer is current".
Coalesce: when a newer push arrives before an older job starts, the older one can be cancelled. Decide what happens if it already started.
Classify failures into transient (retry with backoff) and deterministic (record the error, stop, wait for a new revision).
followups: A maintainer pushes 30 commits in 10 minutes while fixing a file. What runs, what is cancelled, and what do viewers see?
A 300 GB dataset with 40 configurations is pushed. How do you schedule it so that small datasets pushed at the same time still convert within minutes?
A dataset's column is an integer in the first 1 000 files and a string in file 1 001. What does your schema inference do, and what do you tell the owner?
You change the conversion code, and every dataset's shards should be rebuilt. How do you roll that out without the viewer going stale for everyone?
A gated dataset's conditions change so that some users lose access. What must happen to the converted shards and to any caches in front of them?

rules.ask: One {{max_size}} dataset takes hours on a worker. How does your queue keep small datasets flowing while it runs?
Which failures do you retry, and how do you stop retrying a malformed file every hour for months?
You overwrite the converted shards in place. What does a viewer paging through rows see while the overwrite is half done?
How do you choose the row-group size, and what does it do to the cost of serving one random page of 100 rows?
How many rows or files do you read to infer a schema, and what happens when a later file disagrees?

incidents: A release of a popular data library changes how one of the {{formats}} formats is parsed, and conversions that succeeded yesterday start failing for 4% of datasets.
A dataset near {{max_size}} is pushed 12 times in one afternoon, and each push starts a full conversion that the next push makes useless.
A dataset is made private while its conversion is running, and the job finishes and writes shards to a location the viewer serves publicly.

templates.title: Repositories as data — commits, branches, tags, large-file pointers and exactly what a revision contained
templates.subtopic: commit graphs, ref history, per-revision file manifests, large-file pointers

sections.scenario: The hub hosts about {{repos}} repositories of models, datasets and Spaces. Each is a git repository: commits with parents, branches (usually main, sometimes others such as a conversion branch), tags such as v1.0, and a tree of files. In this exercise a file larger than {{pointer_threshold}} is committed as a small pointer that names a large-file object by its SHA-256 and size; the bytes live in large-file storage. Users push about {{daily_commits}} commits a day; branches can be force-pushed, tags can be moved or deleted, and a repository can be renamed or transferred to another owner. A repository can hold up to {{max_files}} files. Analysts, the download-statistics team and support all ask the same kind of question: "what exactly did revision X contain, and what was main on date D?"
sections.problem: Design the analytical data model for repository contents and history. Cover: commits and their parents (merges have two), the history of every ref (branch and tag moves, including force-pushes and deletions), the file manifest of a revision (path, blob id, size, whether it is a pointer and which large-file object it names), how a request "file F at revision R" resolves to bytes when R is a branch, a tag or a commit id, and the facts that answer "files and total bytes in a revision", "which revisions of which repos reference large-file object O", "what main pointed to at a given time" and "commits per repo per day". Say how a manifest is stored without copying {{max_files}} rows for every commit.
sections.constraints: Commit ids and blob ids are content hashes and never change; refs do. History must survive force-pushes: a commit that is no longer reachable from any ref is still answerable for as long as it is retained. Repository identity must survive renames and transfers. Pointer files and the objects they name are separate things: the same object can be named by many paths, revisions and repositories. Times are UTC.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, thresholds and file counts are hypothetical, as are the pointer rule and threshold (this exercise's rule; check current docs). You receive push events (repo id, ref, old commit, new commit, pushed_at) and can read any commit's tree. Private repositories exist; their contents never appear in public analytics.
sections.criteria: Immutable, hash-keyed commits, trees, blobs and large-file objects separated from mutable refs and names; ref history as validity intervals including force-pushes and tag moves; a manifest stored as parent diffs plus checkpoints with a stated reconstruction bound; pointers modelled apart from the objects they name, with a reverse index; repo identity stable across renames and transfers; private content kept out of public facts; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Do I need to store file contents?
clarifications.a: No. Paths, blob ids, sizes and pointer details only.

clarifications.q: Can a tag move?
clarifications.a: In this scenario, yes: an owner can delete a tag and recreate it on another commit. Your model must say which commit the tag named at any time.

clarifications.q: Is a rename a new repository?
clarifications.a: No. The repo keeps a stable id; the owner/name pair has a history.

clarifications.q: How are revisions written in requests?
clarifications.a: As a branch name, a tag name or a full commit id; a short commit prefix is not accepted in this exercise.

clarifications.q: What happens to commits dropped by a force-push?
clarifications.a: They stay in the data for a retention period (your choice, stated), marked unreachable.

hints: Separate what never changes (commits, trees, blobs, large-file objects, all keyed by hash) from what moves (refs and repo names, kept as validity intervals).
A manifest can be stored as the change from the first parent (added, modified, deleted paths) plus periodic full checkpoints; any revision's manifest is a checkpoint plus the changes after it.
"What was main at time T" is an interval lookup on the ref's history, not a property of a commit.
followups: Write the query (in words or SQL) that lists the files and total bytes of main on a given date for one repo, from your tables.
A force-push replaces the last five commits of main. What rows change in your model, and what does a download recorded against the old head now resolve to?
A merge commit has two parents. Which parent do you diff against when storing the manifest, and how do you answer "which commit introduced this path"?
With repositories of up to {{max_files}} files and {{daily_commits}} commits a day, how often do you checkpoint a full manifest, and how do you bound the cost of reconstructing any revision?
A large-file object is named by pointers in thousands of repositories. How do you answer "which public revisions reference it" quickly, and keep private repos out of the answer?

rules.ask: A repo with {{max_files}} files gets a one-line README change. How many rows does your design write, and what does that cost at {{daily_commits}} commits a day?
That records where a branch is now. A download was logged against main three weeks ago; how do you find which commit it meant?
The repo was renamed and later transferred. What is its key in your facts, and how does a dashboard keyed by name keep its history?
Two repos commit the same 4 GB file under different paths. How many large-file objects, pointer rows and manifest entries do you store?
An owner deletes a branch. Which of your rows disappear, which are marked, and what can support still answer afterwards?

incidents: A dashboard of "bytes per model" doubles overnight for repos holding files above {{pointer_threshold}}: the manifest job started counting both the pointer file's size and the large-file object's size for the same path.
After a series of force-pushes on busy repos, a download report resolves branch names with the ref's current head and attributes three weeks of downloads to commits that did not exist yet.
Manifest reconstruction for repos with {{max_files}} files slows to minutes because checkpoints were only written at creation; every lookup replays every change since.

templates.title: Gated repositories — access conditions, requests, approvals, revocations and licence changes
templates.subtopic: access-condition versions, request lifecycles, grants as intervals, licence metadata per revision

sections.scenario: On the hub, a repository owner can gate a model or dataset: a user must accept the owner's access conditions, and may have to fill in a short form (here up to {{form_fields}} fields), before the files can be downloaded. Some owners approve every request automatically (about {{auto_share}} of the {{gated_repos}} gated repos here); others review requests by hand and can reject them or later revoke access. Owners edit their conditions and form over time, and the licence declared in the repo's metadata can change from one revision to the next. About {{daily_requests}} access requests arrive a day. Owners want to see who has access and under which conditions they accepted; users want to see the status of their own requests; the hub's analysts want aggregate review times and approval rates, never form answers.
sections.problem: Design the data model for gating. Cover: the gate configuration and its versions (on/off, manual or automatic approval, the conditions text and form fields), the access request lifecycle (requested, approved, rejected, revoked, and requested again), which conditions version a user accepted, access grants as intervals so "could user U download from repo R at time T" is answerable, how form answers are stored and who can read them, and the licence declared at each revision. Define the facts that answer "median time to decision per repo", "approval rate by approval mode" and "downloads by users whose access was later revoked".
sections.constraints: Every decision keeps who made it (owner, a member of the owning organisation, or the automatic rule) and when. A grant is never edited in place; a revocation closes it. Form answers are personal data: they are readable by the repo's owners and by the user, retained under a stated policy, and never copied into analytics. The licence is metadata the owner declares; the model records what was declared and when, and draws no conclusion about what a licence permits.
sections.assumptions: Counts and shares are hypothetical; gating behaviour here is this exercise's rule (check current docs). A request is made by one user for one repo. An organisation can own repos and has members who can act on requests.
sections.criteria: Versioned gate configuration referenced by each request and acceptance; request lifecycle as decision events with actors; grants as intervals that revocations close; licence declarations per revision with no legal conclusions; form answers isolated with access control and retention, never in analytics; precise time-to-decision definitions split by approval mode with pending handled; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: If the owner changes the conditions, do existing users have to accept again?
clarifications.a: In this scenario the owner chooses per change: "re-accept required" or not. Your model must support both.

clarifications.q: Can a rejected user request again?
clarifications.a: Yes. Each request is its own row; the latest one is the current status.

clarifications.q: Does ungating a repo end all requests?
clarifications.a: Pending requests are closed as "gate removed"; existing grants stay in the history but no longer matter while the repo is ungated.

clarifications.q: Is the licence part of the gate?
clarifications.a: No. It is declared in the repo's metadata at each revision; a gate's conditions can mention it.

clarifications.q: What do analysts see?
clarifications.a: Counts, rates and durations per repo and approval mode, with no form answers and no user-level rows.

hints: Version the gate configuration; every request and acceptance points at the version the user saw.
Keep requests (a lifecycle with typed decision events) apart from grants (validity intervals derived from decisions).
Licence declarations belong to the repository's revision history, not to the gate.
followups: Write how you answer "could user U download from repo R at 14:00 on a given day", including a revocation at 13:00 and a re-approval at 15:00.
The owner adds a field to the form and requires re-acceptance. What happens to existing grants, and how is the transition shown to users and to the owner?
Define "median hours to decision" so automatic and manual repos, pending requests and re-requests are handled consistently.
A user asks for their form answers to be deleted. What is removed, what stays, and how do the owner's audit view and the aggregate facts remain correct?
At {{daily_requests}} requests a day with {{auto_share}} approved automatically, which tables grow fastest, and how do you keep "who has access now" fast for an owner with many users?

rules.ask: A request went pending, approved, revoked, re-requested and approved again. If one status column is overwritten, how do you answer "did this user have access last Tuesday"?
Who can read those rows, how long are they kept, and what stops them leaking into an analytics table?
The declared licence changed between two revisions. Which revision's licence does an access request refer to, and what does your model avoid concluding?
How do automatic approvals appear in "median time to decision"? Should they share a number with manual reviews?
Downloads made before the revocation are still in the logs. How do you report them, and what does the revoked user see?

incidents: An owner's dashboard reports a median of 0 hours to decision for a manually reviewed repo: the repo switched from automatic to manual approval mid-month, and the facts used the current mode for every request.
A nightly export of request data for analysts started including form answers after a schema change added them to the request table as a JSON column.

After an owner revoked access for many users at once, "users with access" stayed flat for a day: grants were derived only from approvals and a nightly job, with {{daily_requests}} requests a day crowding the queue.

templates.title: Model cards and metadata as data — base models, declared datasets, licences and tags over time
templates.subtopic: semi-structured card metadata per revision, normalised relations, vocabularies, temporal queries

sections.scenario: Every model repository can carry a card: a README whose header block holds structured metadata (licence, tags, library, pipeline task, languages, the datasets the model was trained on, and the base model or models it was derived from, with a relation such as fine-tune, adapter, quantised or merge), followed by free text. The {{model_repos}} model repos receive about {{daily_card_edits}} card edits a day, each a commit. About {{base_declared}} of models declare a base model. Metadata is written by people: about {{invalid_share}} of headers contain an unknown tag, a misspelled licence identifier, a dataset that does not exist on the hub, or plain malformed YAML. Search filters, the "models derived from this one" list on a model page and analysts' questions all read this metadata.
sections.problem: Design the data model that turns card headers into queryable data over time. Cover: what is stored per revision (the raw header, the parse result and its errors), the normalised relations (model → base model with relation type, model → dataset, model → tag, model → licence), controlled vocabularies and how unknown values are kept, how references to other repos survive renames, and how to answer "the licence and base model declared on date D", "models whose declared base model changed", "models declaring dataset X, as of now and as of a past date" and "share of cards with a valid header by month". Say what the derivative list reads and how it stays fresh.
sections.constraints: The raw header for every revision is kept; normalised rows can be rebuilt from it when the parser changes. A malformed header never blocks a push and never erases the last good metadata from search. References to other repos are stored by stable repo id where they resolve and as the declared text where they do not. The model records what owners declared, never whether a declaration is true or what a licence permits.
sections.assumptions: Counts and shares are hypothetical. Card edits arrive as commits (repo id, commit, pushed_at, header text). The tag vocabulary and licence identifiers are a curated list that changes a few times a month.
sections.criteria: Raw header kept per revision with a versioned parse result and errors; normalised relations (base model with type, dataset, tag, licence) tied to revisions or validity intervals; declared versus resolved references, keyed by stable repo id; vocabularies versioned without rewriting what owners wrote; last-good metadata preserved for search; no conclusions about truth or licence meaning; freshness of derived views explained; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Should a header that fails to parse appear in search?
clarifications.a: The repo appears with its last valid metadata, marked as having a header error on the current revision.

clarifications.q: Can a model declare several base models?
clarifications.a: Yes, for merges; each relation is its own row with its type.

clarifications.q: What if a declared dataset is later renamed on the hub?
clarifications.a: The reference should still find it; say how.

clarifications.q: Do card edits on non-default branches count?
clarifications.a: Only the default branch drives search and the model page; other branches are kept as history.

clarifications.q: Who reads the free text?
clarifications.a: Nobody in analytics: only its length and the presence of standard sections are measured.

hints: Store the raw header per revision and parse it into versioned rows; normalised relations carry the revision they came from (or validity intervals on the default branch).
Keep "declared value" and "resolved value" side by side: a dataset reference as written, and the repo id it resolved to, if any.
A vocabulary change is a new version of the vocabulary: re-validating old revisions should not rewrite what an owner wrote.
followups: Show the rows written for one card edit that changes the licence, adds a tag that is not in the vocabulary and declares a second base model as a merge.
The parser gets a new version that accepts a previously rejected licence spelling. How do you reprocess, and what changes in last month's "valid header" share?
How do you answer "the base model declared on 1 March" for a model whose card was edited ten times since?
A base model is renamed, then deleted. What does the derivative list on each child show, and what do your relations hold?
With {{daily_card_edits}} edits a day, how do you keep the derivative list and search facets fresh within minutes without re-parsing every card?

rules.ask: Search needs "all models with tag X and licence Y" in milliseconds. What do you index or flatten, and how do you keep it in step with the raw header?
An analyst asks which licence a model declared last March. Where does that come from in your design?
About {{invalid_share}} of headers name things that do not resolve. Does your foreign key reject the row, drop the reference or keep it as text?
Does a header that fails validation block the push? What does the model page show while it is broken?
The derivative list follows declared base models. What happens with a declared cycle, and with a base model that is private?

incidents: A curated licence list was updated and the nightly re-validation re-parsed every revision; about {{invalid_share}} of models suddenly showed "no licence" in search because unknown values were dropped instead of kept as declared text.
A popular base model was renamed; the derivative list on its page went from thousands of models to a handful because relations were keyed by the declared owner/name string.

After a card-template change, merges declared base models as a list in a new field; the parser read only the old single-value field and every merge disappeared from the "models derived from" counts for a week.

templates.title: Spaces — apps, hardware, builds, sleep and wake, duplicates, and secrets that never reach analytics
templates.subtopic: app lifecycle states, builds per commit, hardware intervals, duplication lineage, secret handling

sections.scenario: A Space is an app hosted from a git repository on the hub: the owner chooses an SDK (for example a Python UI framework, a static site or a container), pushes code, and each push triggers a build. A running Space uses one of {{hardware_tiers}} hardware tiers, from a free CPU tier to paid GPU tiers, and the owner can change tier at any time. In this exercise a Space with no visitors sleeps after {{sleep_hours}} hours (owners on paid hardware can choose a different sleep time) and wakes when someone visits; sleep rules are this exercise's rule (check current docs). Users can duplicate a public Space into their own account. Owners store secrets (API keys) and variables in the Space's settings. There are about {{spaces}} Spaces and {{daily_builds}} builds a day. The hub wants to understand build failures, time to first running state, hardware hours by tier and how often duplicated Spaces diverge from their source; owners want their own Space's history.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: Spaces and their repos, builds per commit (queued, building, failed with a classified reason, succeeded), the runtime state history (building, running, sleeping, paused, error, deleted), hardware assignments as intervals, wake events and the time from a visit to running, duplication lineage (which Space and commit a duplicate came from), and settings changes. Define facts for "build failure rate by SDK and reason", "hardware hours by tier per day", "median wake time by tier" and "duplicates whose code no longer matches the source". State exactly how secrets are kept out of every analytical table and log.
sections.constraints: Secret values never leave the secrets store: no analytics table, log line, event payload or build-log extract may contain one. Analytics may record that a secret named X was added, changed or removed, by whom and when. Build logs are owner-visible only; analytics sees a classified failure reason. Hardware hours must be reconstructable for any past day. Times are UTC.
sections.assumptions: Counts, tiers and sleep times are hypothetical. Events arrive from the build system and the runtime as (space_id, kind, at, details). A private Space's details are visible only to its owners; aggregates over all Spaces may include it.
sections.criteria: Separate code, configuration and runtime histories joined by build and configuration versions; runtime state and hardware as intervals; precise wake-time and running definitions; duplication lineage by source Space and commit; build failures classified without log text; secret values confined to the secrets store, with only metadata in analytics and logs; hardware hours from interval overlaps; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Does a settings change rebuild the Space?
clarifications.a: A secret or hardware change restarts it; your model should record which commit and settings version each run used.

clarifications.q: Is a duplicate linked to its source after duplication?
clarifications.a: Only by the record of where it came from; after that it is an independent repo.

clarifications.q: What counts as "running"?
clarifications.a: The first successful health check after a build or wake.

clarifications.q: Can a build log mention a secret?
clarifications.a: User code can print anything. Assume a build log may contain a secret value, which is why it stays out of analytics.

clarifications.q: Is a sleeping Space using hardware?
clarifications.a: No. Hardware hours count only running time.

hints: Keep three histories apart: code (commits and builds), configuration (hardware, sleep time, settings versions), and runtime state (intervals). Each run references a build and a configuration version.
Record secrets by name and fingerprint-free metadata only; never hash a secret value into analytics either.
Hardware hours are the overlap of "running" intervals with hardware-assignment intervals.
followups: Show the rows written when an owner pushes a commit, the build fails, they fix it, it succeeds, and they move to a GPU tier an hour later.
Define "wake time" precisely. Which event starts it, which ends it, and what about a visit while the Space is already waking?
Write how you compute hardware hours by tier for one day, including a Space that slept through midnight and changed tier mid-run.
A Space was duplicated 5,000 times. How do you answer "how many duplicates still run the source's code", and what does "the same code" mean?
An owner reports their secret appeared in a dashboard. Walk through how your design makes that impossible, and what you check first.

rules.ask: Hardware hours for last Tuesday need every running interval. If state is overwritten in place, where do those intervals come from?
Where does the secret value live, which service reads it, and which of your tables could end up containing it by accident?
User code can print a secret in its build output. How does a failure reason reach analytics without the log text?
The source Space is deleted later. What happens to the lineage of its duplicates in your model?
A visitor arrives while the Space is still building after a push. Is that a wake? How does it count in median wake time?

incidents: A build-failure classifier started storing the last 20 lines of each failed build log "for debugging" in the analytics table; several contained API keys that user code printed at startup.

Hardware hours by tier dropped by a third on the day the sleep time changed to {{sleep_hours}} hours: sleep and wake events arrived out of order and the interval builder closed running intervals at the next event of any kind.
With {{daily_builds}} builds a day, a retry storm after a registry outage created several builds per commit; "build failure rate" counted every attempt and doubled for one SDK.

templates.title: Cold starts — requests that reached a scaled-to-zero inference endpoint, and the wait each added
templates.subtopic: state as of an event, interval boundaries, next-event lookups, at-least-once logs

sections.scenario: A team serves {{endpoint_count}} models from the hub on dedicated inference endpoints (table endpoints). An endpoint with min_replicas 0 scales to zero after idle_minutes with no requests, and wakes when a request arrives: the request is held until the first replica is ready (this exercise's rule; check current docs). An endpoint with min_replicas 1 never scales to zero. Scaling is logged in endpoint_events and requests in endpoint_requests; the export covers the UTC day {{day}} and ends at {{cutoff}}. {{kinds_rule}} replica_ready is also logged when autoscaling adds a replica to an endpoint that is already serving. The team wants to know, per endpoint, how many requests hit a cold endpoint and how much waiting the cold starts added, to decide which endpoints should keep one replica warm.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns endpoint_id, requests, cold_requests, waiting_at_end, total_wait_s, max_wait_s: one row per endpoint in endpoints, ordered by endpoint_id. An endpoint's state at a time is set by its latest event with occurred_at at or before that time; before its first event it is serving. {{cold_rule}} A request is cold when the endpoint was at zero at its received_at. A cold request's wait is the number of seconds from its received_at to the endpoint's first replica_ready after received_at; if there is no such event in the export, the request counts in waiting_at_end and has no wait. requests counts the endpoint's requests, cold_requests its cold requests (including those in waiting_at_end), and total_wait_s and max_wait_s are the sum and maximum of the waits, 0 when there are none. {{feed_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The boundaries matter: a request at exactly the second of scaled_to_zero is cold, and a request at exactly the second of replica_ready is served. Two events of the same endpoint never share a second. The sample has {{events}} events and {{requests}} request rows; production holds billions of requests a month across many endpoints.
