sections.assumptions: Hypothetical endpoints, repos, instance types, times and rules. Timestamps are whole seconds. logged_at is when the request row reached the log store and plays no part in the state.
sections.criteria: State taken from the latest event at or before each request with exactly the stated boundaries; autoscaling replica_ready not mistaken for a wake; the wait ended by the first replica_ready after arrival, not by a failed start; open cold periods counted as waiting with no wait; every endpoint present via a LEFT JOIN from endpoints; at the hardest level, paused requests not cold, resumed treated as at zero, and one row per request_id; deterministic ordering; can explain interval precomputation and percentiles.

clarifications.q: Is a request that arrives right before an autoscaling replica_ready a cold start?
clarifications.a: No. The endpoint was serving when it arrived; the new replica only adds capacity.

clarifications.q: Does idle_minutes enter the query?
clarifications.a: No. The events already record when each endpoint scaled to zero; idle_minutes explains why.

clarifications.q: Should endpoints with no requests appear?
clarifications.a: Yes, with zeros. The decision is about every endpoint.

clarifications.q: Which replica_ready ends a cold request's wait?
clarifications.a: The first one strictly after the request arrived. Failed starts in between do not end it.

clarifications.q: How do I get whole seconds from two timestamps?
clarifications.a: EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM later - earlier) returns seconds.

hints: For each request, find the endpoint's latest event at or before received_at (a LATERAL subquery with ORDER BY … DESC LIMIT 1, or a window over a union of events and requests). That kind decides cold or not.
For cold requests, find the first replica_ready strictly after received_at; a missing one means the request was still waiting at the end.
Aggregate per endpoint with COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …), starting from endpoints with a LEFT JOIN.
followups: Rewrite the state lookup without LATERAL, using window functions over a union of events and requests. What breaks if an event and a request share a second?
At billions of requests a month, how would you precompute the at-zero intervals per endpoint so this becomes a range join, and which index or clustering serves it?
Add the p90 wait per endpoint. Which aggregate do you use in PostgreSQL, and what changes in an engine without an exact percentile?
The team wants the cost of keeping one replica warm against the waits it would save. What extra data do you need, and what assumption about traffic does the comparison make?

rules.ask: The next event after a request can be an autoscaling replica_ready while the endpoint is serving. Does your LEAD/LAG approach call that request cold?
Which endpoints disappear when you start from the requests, and are any of them ones the decision needs?
BETWEEN includes both ends. What does it do to a request at exactly the second a replica became ready?
Why can logged_at be later than received_at, and which of the two belongs in the state lookup?
After a failed start, is the endpoint still at zero? Which event ends the wait of a request that arrived after the failure?
What exactly does your DISTINCT remove? Two genuine requests can arrive at the same second for the same endpoint.

incidents: A status-code dashboard showed almost no cold starts on {{day}} because held requests eventually returned success; this query, which reads scaling events, showed several endpoints adding minutes of waiting, longer than many callers were willing to wait.
An earlier version of this report paired each scale-to-zero with the next event of any kind; on days with failed starts it showed short waits exactly when callers saw the longest ones.
A log-store consumer restart redelivered request rows; a version that counted raw rows inflated cold requests on the busiest endpoints and the team nearly paid for warm replicas that were not needed.

templates.title: Download analytics at hub scale with a published counting rule
templates.subtopic: published counting rules, bots and mirrors, restatements

sections.scenario: An open hub hosts {{repos}} public model and dataset repositories. Every file a client fetches is a request at the hub's download edge, {{daily_requests}} file requests a day in total. Fetching one model usually means many requests: a configuration file, a tokenizer, several weight shards, sometimes the same files again on every run. Each repository page shows a download count for the last 30 days and all-time, and authors quote these numbers in papers and launch posts. Some clients are not people at all: CI jobs that re-fetch on every build, caching mirrors run by companies and universities (known mirrors account for {{mirror_share}} of all requests), and crawlers.
sections.problem: Design the download analytics system. Define the counting rule you would publish (which requests count as one download, in this exercise's terms), and design the path from raw edge request logs to per-repository counts, the per-repository dashboard, the exclusion of mirrors and automated traffic, and restatements: how a count is corrected when a source of bad traffic is found later, going back at most {{restate_days}} days.
sections.constraints: A repository page reads its counts in under 50 ms at p99. Counts may lag by up to a day, but a provisional number for today should appear within an hour. Raw logs contain network addresses and client identifiers; nothing that identifies a person may be kept longer than this exercise's 30-day raw-log retention, and per-user download lists are never shown to anyone. The rule must be published so that an author can check, in principle, why a number is what it is.
sections.assumptions: All volumes and shares are hypothetical. In this exercise a repository can designate which of its files count (a configuration file by default), and a library can declare the designated files for the repositories that use it; check current docs for the hub's actual rule. The mirror list is maintained by the hub and changes a few times a month.
sections.criteria: Publishes an explicit, versioned counting rule (designated files, repeat collapsing per client and day, excluded categories) and implements it as one function; separates a provisional fast count from an exact daily recomputation; client de-duplication that respects retention (rotating salted identifiers, no per-user lists); mirrors and automated clients handled through a maintained registry with effective dates and shown as excluded shares; restatements as new versions with a visible changelog on the repository and a stated limit; serving from precomputed aggregates; monitors on ratios (designated to all file requests, per library version) that catch client changes; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, correction and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does fetching ten weight shards count as ten downloads?
clarifications.a: Under this exercise's rule only requests for designated files count, so a normal fetch counts once; you decide how repeats are collapsed and say why.

clarifications.q: Do HEAD requests and cache revalidations count?
clarifications.a: Your call. State what you count, and what a client that checks for updates on every run does to your number.

clarifications.q: Should mirrors count at all?
clarifications.a: One fetch by a mirror can serve thousands of people the hub never sees. Decide whether to exclude, count once, or show separately, and publish it.

clarifications.q: Who can see per-country or per-organisation breakdowns?
clarifications.a: Nobody, in this exercise. Authors see totals, a daily series and the share of traffic excluded, by reason.

clarifications.q: Can a count ever go down?
clarifications.a: Yes, after a restatement. Say how the author finds out.

hints: Write the counting rule down first as a function from one request to "counts", "excluded (reason)" or "ignored". Everything else implements and versions that function.
Keep two paths: an approximate, fast provisional count and an exact daily count recomputed from retained logs. Only the daily count is final.
A restatement is a new version of a day's numbers, not an edit. Keep enough per-day detail (counted and excluded, by reason and rule version) that you can recompute or explain any day.
followups: Walk one request for a designated file from the edge log to the number on the repository page. Where can it be counted twice, and what stops that?
How do you collapse repeated fetches by the same client in a day without keeping a per-user list longer than the retention allows?
A university mirror asks to be removed from the mirror list because it wants its users counted. What do you need before you agree, and what changes in the numbers?
A bot source is identified today that has been active longer than {{restate_days}} days. How do you correct what you can, and what do you say about the days you cannot?
An author says their count dropped by half overnight with no change to their repository. How do you investigate, and what monitor would have caught it first?

rules.ask: Your sketch has about 1% error. Is a final, published count allowed to be approximate, and does the error matter for a repository with 40 downloads?
Most fetches are anonymous. What identifies a client for de-duplication, and how long do you keep it?
An author asks what the number was before last month's correction. Where does your design keep that?
Which number on the page comes from the stream, which from the daily job, and what happens when they disagree?
A CI system changes its client string every release. How does your exclusion keep up, and how do you know it has fallen behind?

incidents: A popular CI template starts fetching one model's designated file on every job without a cache. That model's counted downloads rise forty-fold in two days, and its author cites the number in a launch post before anyone notices.

A new release of a widely used client library skips the designated file when its local cache is warm. Counted downloads for thousands of repositories fall by a third on the day it ships, while total file requests do not fall.

One of the listed mirrors, which on its own carries a large part of the {{mirror_share}} mirror traffic, changes its client identifier without notice, and for a week its requests are counted as ordinary downloads.
A network of automated clients is identified whose traffic began before the oldest day you restate ({{restate_days}} days back); some repositories' all-time counts are inflated by it.

templates.title: Inference endpoint telemetry with scale-to-zero and cold starts
templates.subtopic: autoscaling, scale-to-zero, cold starts, per-endpoint latency

sections.scenario: Customers deploy models from an open hub as dedicated inference endpoints. For each endpoint they pick hardware, a minimum and maximum number of replicas, and an autoscaling target; the platform adds replicas as load per replica rises and removes them as it falls. In this exercise an endpoint with a minimum of zero scales to zero after {{idle_minutes}} minutes without requests, and the next request waits for a cold start: a replica is scheduled, its image pulled, the model weights fetched and loaded onto the accelerator (this exercise's rule; check current docs). There are {{endpoints}} endpoints across {{regions}} regions, serving {{peak_rps}} requests per second at peak in total. Each request passes a router in front of the endpoint's replicas.
sections.problem: Design the telemetry system. Customers need, per endpoint: request rate, latency percentiles, errors by kind, replica count over time, and every cold start with how long it took and how many requests it delayed. The platform needs fleet-wide views and an audit of every autoscaling decision with the inputs that caused it. Cover what is emitted (router, replicas, lifecycle events, autoscaler), how it is collected across regions, stored and queried, and how late or missing data is shown.
sections.constraints: Dashboards are at most one minute behind. Full-resolution data is kept 30 days and coarser data for a year. Request and response bodies are customer data and never enter telemetry; only metadata does. Telemetry must keep working, and say so honestly, when a region's collectors fall behind.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, timings and targets are hypothetical. Replicas expose a health check; the router knows how many requests are queued per endpoint. Customers may run very different models, so a cold start can take seconds or many minutes.
sections.criteria: Measures at the router (client-perceived latency, queueing, rejections) as well as at replicas; replica lifecycle as an event log from which cold starts and their phases are derived; mergeable histograms with bounded label cardinality; an autoscaler decision log with inputs and policy version; regional collection with event-time handling and an explicit "data delayed" state; no request or response content in telemetry; tiered retention and cost control for idle endpoints; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Where is latency measured?
clarifications.a: You decide, but customers care about what their clients experienced, including time spent waiting for a replica.

clarifications.q: Is a request that times out while an endpoint is waking an error of the endpoint?
clarifications.a: It is something the customer must be able to see and explain. Decide how it is labelled.

clarifications.q: How detailed is the autoscaling audit?
clarifications.a: For each decision: time, endpoint, old and new replica counts, the metric values and target that drove it, and the policy version.

clarifications.q: Can customers export their telemetry?
clarifications.a: Yes, as metrics and as a stream of lifecycle events.

hints: Model each replica's life as a sequence of events (scheduled, image pulled, weights loaded, ready, unhealthy, terminated). A cold start is a span you can derive from those events plus the router's queue.
Percentiles cannot be averaged across replicas or regions. Store mergeable histograms and compute percentiles at query time.
Distinguish "zero" from "no data". A dashboard that draws missing data as zero turns a collection delay into a fake outage.
followups: Define a cold start precisely: when does it begin, when does it end, and which requests are attributed to it?
Estimate the number of time series and points per second at {{endpoints}} endpoints, and say which labels you refuse to put on a metric.
How do customers see requests the router rejected or timed out while no replica existed?
The autoscaler and the dashboard disagree about how busy an endpoint was. Which one is right, and how would you prove it?
How would you reduce what telemetry costs per idle endpoint, given that most endpoints are idle most of the time?

rules.ask: Average latency hides cold starts. Which percentile does a customer with occasional cold starts care about, and how do you compute it across replicas?
While an endpoint has zero replicas there is nothing to emit from. Where do the failed requests of that period show up?
A replica lives for forty seconds before it crashes. Does your scrape interval ever see it?
At {{peak_rps}} requests per second, how long can you afford to keep per-request records, and what do you keep instead?
What exactly in your telemetry could contain customer data, and what stops it from getting there?

incidents: An endpoint serving a large model takes eleven minutes to become ready after scaling to zero. Its clients see timeouts the whole time, but the endpoint's dashboard shows no requests and no errors for those minutes, because only replicas report metrics.

One replica of a busy endpoint restarts in a loop after running out of accelerator memory on long inputs. The endpoint's error rate stays under 1% because the router retries elsewhere, but latency doubles and the autoscaler still counts the replica as capacity.

Collectors in one of the {{regions}} regions fall 35 minutes behind. Dashboards for its endpoints show them idle, and customers whose minimum is zero ask whether their endpoints scaled down after {{idle_minutes}} minutes.

templates.title: Large-file storage for repositories: deduplication, garbage collection and quotas
templates.subtopic: content addressing, cross-fork deduplication, safe garbage collection, quotas

sections.scenario: Repositories on an open hub are git repositories, but large files (weights, dataset shards) are stored outside git: the commit holds a small pointer naming the file's content hash and size, and the bytes live in an object store addressed by that hash. The hub holds {{stored}} of large files and receives {{daily_upload}} of new uploads a day before deduplication. Duplication is everywhere: forks, re-uploads of the same weights under a new name, fine-tunes that change a few layers, datasets that append shards. In a sample, {{fork_share}} of newly pushed large-file bytes already existed somewhere on the hub. Users delete files, branches and whole repositories, and sometimes rewrite history to reclaim space. Each account has a storage quota.
sections.problem: Design large-file storage for repositories: how objects are addressed, uploaded and verified; how duplicates are stored once (whole files, and optionally parts of files); how storage no longer referenced by any branch, tag or retained revision is reclaimed safely, with a grace period of {{grace_days}} days; and how storage is counted against quotas when one object is shared by many repositories and accounts.
sections.constraints: A byte referenced by any commit reachable from a branch or tag must never be deleted. Downloads verify the content hash. An upload of a file that already exists should not transfer it again. Quota numbers shown to a user must be explainable from their own repositories.
sections.assumptions: All sizes, rates and shares are hypothetical. In this exercise clients upload large-file bytes first and then push the commit that references them; a long upload can take hours. Check current docs for how the hub actually stores large files.
sections.criteria: Content-addressed objects with hash verification on write and read; upload protocol that checks existence first and commits only after bytes are durable; deduplication at file level with a reasoned choice about content-defined chunks and their index; a reference index or periodic mark from all retained refs instead of fragile per-object counts; two-phase deletion (candidate, grace, delete) where any new reference, including a dedup hit, cancels the deletion atomically; a published quota rule for shared objects that users can verify; scrubbing and repair from replicas; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Whole-file or chunk-level deduplication?
clarifications.a: Your choice. Say what each saves for a fine-tune that changes 5% of a model's bytes, and what each costs in metadata.

clarifications.q: Does deleting a branch delete its files?
clarifications.a: Only when nothing else still references them. Revisions reachable from another branch or tag, or from another repository, keep them.

clarifications.q: Are private repositories deduplicated against public ones?
clarifications.a: Decide. Say whether dedup could reveal to someone that a private file exists.

clarifications.q: Does a fork count against the forker's quota?
clarifications.a: Your rule; publish it and make sure the forker can understand it.

hints: Content addressing makes deduplication and integrity checks the same mechanism: the address is the hash of the bytes.
A reference index (which commits point at which objects) maintained on every push and delete is easier to keep correct than a reference count per object.
The dangerous moment in garbage collection is an object that looks unreferenced while an upload or a deduplicated push is about to reference it again.
followups: Walk through uploading a 300 GB checkpoint where 90% of the bytes already exist on the hub. What is transferred, what is written, and when does the commit become visible?
How does garbage collection decide an object can go, and what makes it safe against an upload that finishes just after the decision?
A fine-tune changes a few layers in the middle of a large file. What would chunk-level deduplication need so that an insertion does not change every chunk after it?
Define the quota rule for shared objects. What does an organisation see after it rewrites history on a repository that has hundreds of forks?
How would you find out that a stored object's bytes no longer match its hash before a user does?

rules.ask: A delete and a fork happen at the same moment on a repository holding a 200 GB file. Walk through how the count can end up wrong, and what that costs.
How many chunks does {{stored}} come to at your chunk size, and where does the index for them live?
A user deletes a repository by mistake and asks for it back the next morning. What can you restore?
Charging physical bytes means the first uploader pays and every later one is free. Is that the incentive you want?
How many objects is that, and what does listing them all for garbage collection cost?

incidents: Garbage collection deletes an object that a push referenced minutes earlier. The object had been unreferenced for longer than {{grace_days}} days, and the new upload skipped transferring it because deduplication found it still present, in the window between the collector's decision and its delete.
A user forks a 700 GB model to fix one line of its model card and is told they are over quota, although no new large-file bytes were stored.
An organisation squashes the history of a large repository to free space; its usage barely drops, because {{fork_share}} of those bytes are also referenced by forks and other repositories.
A storage node returns bytes for a popular weights file that do not match the file's hash. Downloads of that file fail intermittently for an hour before anyone looks.

templates.title: Scanning pushed files for unsafe formats and committed secrets
templates.subtopic: content scanning queues, rescans, results on the repository

sections.scenario: An open hub accepts {{pushes_per_hour}} pushed files an hour from anyone with an account and holds {{files_total}} files in total. Every pushed file is scanned. Some model files use serialisation formats that can run code when they are loaded (for example, Python pickle-based checkpoints), so a scanner inspects them without loading them and reports what they would import or call; other formats store only tensors and metadata. Text files are scanned for committed credentials such as access tokens and keys, and all files for known malicious content. Each file's status appears on the repository page: no issue found, flagged (with a reason), not yet scanned, or scan failed. The scanners' rules are updated {{rule_releases}}, and a rule update can change the result for files already scanned.
sections.problem: Design the scanning pipeline: how pushes become scan jobs, how jobs are queued, prioritised and run, how results are stored and shown on repository pages, how rescans after a rule update are scheduled, and how owners are told about findings. A new file's status should be known within {{scan_minutes}} minutes. Describe detection only in general terms; the design is about the pipeline, not about the rules.
sections.constraints: Scanners never execute or load the files they scan, and run isolated with limits on memory and time. A detected credential is shown only to the repository's owners, never publicly, and its value never enters logs or analytics. Every change of a file's status is kept with its scanner and rule version, so the history of a warning can be explained.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, rates and timings are hypothetical. Large files are content-addressed, so the same bytes in many repositories have one content hash. Check current docs for how the hub actually scans files and what it shows.
sections.criteria: Push events turned into idempotent jobs keyed by content hash and rule version; separate lanes for new pushes and rescans with fair shares per repository or organisation; isolated scanners with resource limits and a bounded-attempt poison-message policy ending in an explicit "scan failed" status; a results store with history of status changes and versions, joined to file pages through the pointer's hash; private, de-duplicated owner notifications that never carry the secret; a dispute workflow with audit; monitoring of time-to-status, backlog age and per-rule finding rates with a release guard for new rules; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is the push blocked until the scan finishes?
clarifications.a: No, in this exercise pushes are accepted and the status shows "not yet scanned" until a result exists. Say what a downloader sees meanwhile.

clarifications.q: Are identical files in different repositories scanned separately?
clarifications.a: Your decision; say how a result is shared and what happens if the repositories have different owners.

clarifications.q: Who can dispute a finding?
clarifications.a: The repository owner. A dispute is reviewed by people and can override a result for that file and rule version.

clarifications.q: What happens to a credential found in an old commit?
clarifications.a: It stays in history unless the owner rewrites it; the owner must be told so they can revoke it.

hints: Key results by (content hash, scanner, rule version). The same bytes need scanning once per rule version, however many repositories hold them.
New pushes and rescans compete for the same scanners. Give them separate lanes with explicit shares, so a rescan can never starve fresh uploads.
A file that crashes the scanner every time is a poison message. Decide in advance how many attempts it gets and what status it ends with.
followups: Trace one pushed checkpoint from the push to the status on its file page. Which steps are idempotent, and what happens if a worker dies halfway?
A rule release arrives. How long does rescanning {{files_total}} files take with your capacity, and in what order would you rescan?
How do you notify an owner about a committed credential without the notification itself exposing it?
A finding is overturned on dispute. What changes on the page, in the history, and in the numbers you report about flagged files?
How would you notice that a new rule is producing far too many findings before owners are flooded with them?

rules.ask: A 200 GB push now waits on a scan before it is accepted. What does the uploader see, and what happens when the scanners are behind?
One repository pushes 50,000 small files at once. How does your queue keep that from delaying everyone else's scans?
The same file fails on every attempt. What status does its page show after the last one, and who is told?
A rule flags 10,000 files in one organisation overnight. How many messages do its owners get?
Two repositories share a file, and one owner wins a dispute about it. Does the other repository's warning disappear too?

incidents: A rule release queues a rescan of all {{files_total}} files on the same queue as new pushes. Fresh uploads wait nine hours, far beyond {{scan_minutes}} minutes, and their pages say "not yet scanned".
A malformed file makes the scanner run out of memory. The job is retried without limit, and its partition of the queue stops moving for half a day.
A credential rule released {{rule_releases}} starts matching long hexadecimal strings. A dataset of file checksums produces two million findings and floods one owner with notifications.
A popular model is flagged by mistake and shows a warning for a week before a dispute overturns it; its owner asks how many people saw the warning and what will stop it happening again.

templates.title: Discussions, pull requests and moderation on repositories
templates.subtopic: notifications fan-out, moderation queues, per-repo community metrics

sections.scenario: On an open hub every repository has a community tab: discussions, and pull requests that propose commits on a separate reference for a maintainer to review and merge. {{active_repos}} repositories have community activity, with {{comments_per_day}} comments a day. Users watch repositories and follow people and organisations, and are notified in the app and by email about mentions, replies, new pull requests and new releases from what they follow; the most-followed organisation has {{top_followers}} followers. Anyone can report a comment, discussion or repository; in this exercise reports are reviewed within {{report_hours}} hours, and moderators can hide content or restrict accounts. Maintainers see community metrics for their repositories.
sections.problem: Design the community system: the data model for threads, comments, pull requests and their state changes; notification fan-out to watchers and followers, in the app and by email; moderation from report to decision, and what a decision does everywhere the content has already gone; and per-repository community metrics (open threads, time to first maintainer response, pull requests merged) that stay correct when content is hidden, deleted or found to be spam.
sections.constraints: A mention or a reply reaches the person within a minute; announcements to followers within 15 minutes. Hidden content disappears from the repository page, search and any notification not yet sent. Repositories can be renamed or transferred without breaking threads or links. Metrics must be explainable: a maintainer can see which threads a number counts.
sections.assumptions: All volumes and targets are hypothetical. Accounts can be new and unverified. Check current docs for how the hub's discussions and pull requests actually behave.
sections.criteria: An event-log data model keyed by stable ids (repositories, threads, comments) with projections for pages, search, notifications and metrics; hybrid fan-out with separate priority lanes so announcements never delay mentions; delayed, batched email for low-priority notifications so moderation can still catch them; moderation as events applied to every projection, with evidence retained for appeals; spam controls described generally (new-account limits, burst detection, holds) with a plan for launch-day spikes; metrics recomputable from the log with exclusions and a precise definition of maintainer response; renames and transfers handled by ids and redirects; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is a pull request here the same as on a code host?
clarifications.a: Close enough: commits on a separate reference, with comments and a merge by a maintainer. You may treat it as a thread with a reference attached.

clarifications.q: Who counts as a maintainer for "first maintainer response"?
clarifications.a: Anyone with write access to the repository at the time of the response. Decide what happens when access changes.

clarifications.q: Do followers of an organisation get every new repository?
clarifications.a: They get new public repositories and releases; you can batch them into a digest.

clarifications.q: Are reports anonymous?
clarifications.a: To the reported person, yes. Moderators see who reported.

hints: Store threads and comments as an append-only log of events keyed by a stable repository id; pages, notifications, search and metrics are projections of that log.
Fan-out on write is cheap for small audiences and ruinous for {{top_followers}} followers; fan-out on read is the reverse. Most systems mix them.
A moderation decision is itself an event that every projection must apply, including ones that already copied the content somewhere.
followups: Walk a mention in a comment from the moment it is posted to the notification. What is the path, and where can it be delayed by somebody else's traffic?
How do you deliver one announcement to {{top_followers}} followers without delaying everyone's mentions?
A report arrives about a comment that has already been sent by email to 3,000 watchers. What can you still undo, and what do you change so it happens less?
Define "median time to first maintainer response" precisely. What does it do when spam threads are removed a week later?
How would you detect a coordinated spam wave early, without blocking a real launch that brings thousands of new users at once?

rules.ask: The organisation with {{top_followers}} followers posts. How many writes is that, how long do they take, and what waits behind them?
Two million users follow one organisation and half are offline. Where do their notifications wait, and for how long?
Moderators need the evidence for an appeal after the content is removed from view. Where does it live, and who can see it?
A repository is renamed and transferred to another owner. Which of your keys still find its threads?
Five hundred spam threads are removed from a repository a week later. How does your counter learn about it?

incidents: The organisation with {{top_followers}} followers publishes a model. Notification fan-out builds a backlog, and every user's notifications, mentions included, arrive three hours late.
New accounts open discussions on 50,000 repositories within an hour. The moderation queue grows far past {{report_hours}} hours, and the community metrics of the affected repositories jump.
A comment hidden by a moderator still appears in search results for a day and in emails that had already been queued.

A repository with hundreds of open pull requests is transferred to a new organisation; links in old notifications return not found, and its "first maintainer response" times attribute replies to people who no longer have access.

templates.title: A widely downloaded dataset is found to contain personal data
templates.subtopic: personal data in a published dataset, containment, downstream users

pii: email addresses and phone numbers inside free-text posts
names and home addresses in scanned forms
people's full names next to health details they described
reporter: an outside researcher, in a public discussion on the dataset's repository
a person who found their own details in it, by email
a user of the dataset, privately

sections.scenario: You lead the data engineering team of an organisation that publishes datasets on an open hub. One of your text datasets, built from public web pages two years ago, has been downloaded about {{downloads}} times, and {{derived}} public models declare it as training data in their model cards. Today a report arrives from {{reporter}}: some rows contain {{pii}}. The dataset is a git repository: every revision is kept, and many users pin a specific revision in their training code.
sections.problem: What do you do in the first hour, the first day and the following weeks? Cover how you confirm and size the problem, what you change on the hub and when, what happens to earlier revisions, who you tell (users, authors of derived models, the people in the data, your own organisation's privacy and legal advisers) and what you tell them, and what you change so the next dataset does not ship with the same problem. Then tell me about a real time you handled a data incident involving personal data, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You cannot recall copies already downloaded. Whether and whom you must notify is for your privacy and legal advisers to determine; your job is to give them facts quickly and act on their advice. Many research pipelines depend on the dataset and will break if it disappears.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical. In this exercise a dataset owner can make a repository private or gated, push a new revision, and ask the hub to remove old revisions from history; check current docs for what the hub actually supports.
sections.criteria: First hour: acknowledge the reporter, hide or edit any public comment that repeats the data, verify the report, and take a containment decision (gating or making the repository private) with its cost to users stated; first day: scan the whole dataset to size the problem, engage privacy and legal advisers with facts, prepare a clean revision and a plan for history (removal of old revisions, converted copies); weeks: notify users and derived-model authors through the card, a discussion post and direct contact, without repeating the data; a root-cause review of the filter with measured recall on a labelled sample and a pre-publication review step; no legal conclusions of their own; real example with own actions, measurable outcome and lessons, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: How many rows are affected?
clarifications.a: Unknown. The report shows a dozen rows; nobody has scanned the rest.

clarifications.q: Was the dataset filtered for personal data when it was built?
clarifications.a: A pattern-based filter ran, and its configuration is in the build code.

clarifications.q: Is the report public?
clarifications.a: Depends on the reporter; if it is a public discussion, the comment itself quotes one of the rows.

clarifications.q: Who owns the dataset?
clarifications.a: Your team built and published it under your organisation's account.

hints: Separate containment (stop further spread of the affected rows) from repair (a clean revision) from notification (who must know); they run on different clocks.
A new revision does not remove old ones. Think about history, pinned revisions, the dataset viewer and any converted copies.
Measure before you speak: a scan of the whole dataset turns "some rows" into a number you can act and report on.
followups: Restricting access now protects people in the data but breaks pipelines for thousands of users. How do you decide, and how fast?
How would you size the problem across the whole dataset within a day, and how sure would you be of the number?
What do you say, and where, to the authors of the {{derived}} derived models?
Your filter missed these rows two years ago. What changes in how your team builds and reviews datasets, and how would you know it works?
In your real example, what was the first decision you made, and what would you do differently?

rules.ask: Deleting it breaks every pinned pipeline and erases the evidence of what was published. What do you keep, and where?
The affected rows are still in every earlier revision, and many users pin one. What do you do about history?
While you wait for advice, what can you do on your own authority in the first hour?
Your patterns missed these rows once. How do you estimate how many they still miss?
How do you describe the problem publicly without repeating the personal data or pointing people to where it is?

templates.title: The community's most-requested feature conflicts with an access or safety obligation
templates.subtopic: community demand versus repository conditions, privacy and safety

feature: one-click copying of any model, gated ones included, into the user's own account
showing on each model's page which named organisations download it most
letting repository owners hide the warnings that file scanning shows on their files

sections.scenario: You lead engineering for one area of an open hub of models, datasets and apps. The most-upvoted request in the public feedback forum, with {{votes}} votes, is {{feature}}. It would be simple to build, a competitor offers something similar, and your product manager wants it on the roadmap within {{weeks}} weeks. You believe it conflicts with an obligation the hub has to someone who is not voting: authors of gated repositories who set conditions for access, the people and organisations whose downloads would be shown, or the users who rely on warnings to decide what to load.
sections.problem: How do you handle this? Cover how you establish what the obligation actually is and who decides it, how you work out what the voters really need, what you propose instead or in addition, how the decision is made and communicated publicly, and how you would measure whether the community's need was met. Then tell me about a real time you argued against a popular request, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You do not decide alone: product, policy and legal advisers have a say, and you must not substitute your own legal conclusions for theirs. The forum thread is public, and whatever you decide will be read by the people who asked.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical. In this exercise a repository may require users to accept conditions before access; check current docs for how the hub's gated repositories actually work.
sections.criteria: Separates the stated request from the underlying need, with evidence (forum analysis, a few conversations, usage data); identifies the affected party and brings them, or the policy owners, into the decision; brings facts to legal and policy advisers rather than legal conclusions; proposes variants that serve the need while keeping the obligation (for example copying that carries gating conditions with it, aggregated rather than named download breakdowns, warnings that owners can annotate or dispute but not hide); a clear decision owner and a public explanation with an alternative and a date; a success measure for the need; real example with own actions, cost and lessons, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Why do people want it?
clarifications.a: The thread is long; the most common reasons are convenience and speed, and some posts describe a different underlying problem.

clarifications.q: Have the affected parties been asked?
clarifications.a: No. The repository authors or organisations concerned have not been part of the discussion.

clarifications.q: Is the conflict certain?
clarifications.a: You believe so; policy and legal advisers have not looked at it yet.

clarifications.q: Can the feature be partly built?
clarifications.a: Yes. Any variant is open, including not building it.

hints: Find the job behind the request: what do voters do today without the feature, and what does it cost them?
Name the party whose obligation is at stake and ask them, or their representatives, before deciding for them.
A no in a public forum needs a reason and an alternative; silence reads as indifference.
followups: How would you find out what the {{votes}} voters actually need, beyond what the request says?
What variant would meet most of that need without breaking the obligation?
The product manager says the competitor already does it and nobody complained. How do you respond?
How would you explain the decision in the public thread, and what would you do if the thread turned hostile?
In your real example, what did saying no or changing the request cost, and what did you learn?

rules.ask: Your survey goes to the people who voted. How do you hear from the people the feature would affect, who did not vote?
Who carries the cost if the feature goes wrong, and were they asked?
Whose setting is it: the voter's, or the party the obligation protects? Who should have to opt in?
What do you bring to the policy and legal advisers so they can decide quickly, and what do you do in the meantime?
How much does the competitor's choice tell you about your obligations?

templates.title: Maintaining a widely used open-source library with a small team
templates.subtopic: review capacity, contributors, releases, saying no

pressure: a large company asks for a breaking API change and offers two of its engineers to build it
a security report arrives during a release freeze
the most active outside contributor asks for commit rights

sections.scenario: You lead a team of {{team}} maintainers for an open-source library that many projects on an open hub use to load and process models and datasets. It has had {{contributors}} outside contributors, and {{open_prs}} pull requests are open, some for over a year. Releases are irregular, CI is slow and flaky, and regular contributors have started to drift away. This week, {{pressure}}.
sections.problem: How do you get the project healthy, and how do you handle this week's pressure? Cover review capacity and triage, what you say no to and how, contribution guidelines and CI, release and deprecation policy, how outside contributors gain responsibility, and how you keep your own team from burning out. Then tell me about a real time you maintained or led a project with many outside contributors, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The team will not grow this year. Users depend on the library's API staying stable between major versions. Anything you decide is visible in public issues and pull requests.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Measures the backlog (age, arrival rate, review time) and triages it with labels, clear closes with thanks and reasons, and owners per area; fixes CI speed and flakiness as a multiplier on review capacity; publishes contribution guidelines, a release cadence and a deprecation policy tied to semantic versions; handles the pressure on its merits (a breaking change through a deprecation path and design review regardless of who offers the engineers; security reports privately with coordinated disclosure; graduated responsibility for a contributor); protects the team (rotations for triage, saying no); success measures such as time to first response, pull request age and contributor retention; real example with own actions, measures and lessons, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: What share of open pull requests are still relevant?
clarifications.a: Unknown; nobody has looked at the oldest ones in months.

clarifications.q: Is there a written governance or contribution policy?
clarifications.a: A short contributing guide, out of date.

clarifications.q: Does anyone outside the team have merge rights?
clarifications.a: No.

clarifications.q: How long does CI take?
clarifications.a: About 50 minutes, and one run in five fails for reasons unrelated to the change.

hints: A backlog of reviews is a queue: measure arrivals, review time and age before deciding how to drain it.
Saying no early and kindly costs a contributor less than silence for a year.
Responsibility can be given in steps: triage rights, review rights, ownership of one area, then merge rights.
followups: What do you do with the {{open_prs}} open pull requests in the next month?
How do you respond to this week's pressure, and who else is involved in the decision?
What release and deprecation policy would you publish, and how do you hold to it?
How would you know a year from now that the project is healthier? Name the measures.
In your real example, what did you stop doing, and what happened?

rules.ask: Closing a two-year-old pull request from a first-time contributor without a word: what does that do to the next one, and how would you close it instead?
The team will not grow this year. What do you do with the people you already have, inside and outside the team?
Thousands of projects pin your library. How long is the deprecation window, and how do you tell them?
What does someone have to show before getting that access, and how would you take it back if needed?
Who sees the report, where is the fix developed, and when is it made public?

templates.title: Fixing an interview process on your team that keeps rejecting strong candidates
templates.subtopic: interview process evidence, calibration, structured assessment

signal: two people your team turned down were hired by other teams nearby and are now among their strongest engineers
only 3% of candidates pass your team's take-home exercise, and most who pass decline the offer
your last eight rejections all failed the same live-coding round, which no current team member has ever taken

sections.scenario: You are a senior engineer on a data platform team for an open hub of models and datasets, and you run your team's interview process: the rounds you and your teammates design, run and score when your team hires. The team has {{openings}} open roles and has filled none in {{months}} months. Then {{signal}}. Your manager asks you to fix the process without lowering the bar. This is about the interview process on your own team, not about any real company's hiring process.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you find out what is actually wrong (with evidence rather than impressions), what you change in the rounds, the scoring and the interviewers, how you would know the changes worked, and how you bring the team with you. Then tell me about a real time you changed how a team assessed candidates or other people's work, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You cannot change company-wide hiring policy; you can change your team's rounds, rubrics, interviewer assignments and debriefs. Candidates' personal information stays inside the hiring system; your analysis uses outcomes and scores, not names.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Diagnoses with evidence (funnel by round and interviewer, score distributions, offer acceptance, time to decision, the signal in the scenario treated as a sample); defines what each round measures against the job and rewrites rounds as work samples with written rubrics; calibrates interviewers (shadowing, paired scoring, periodic calibration on the same answer); fixes the debrief (independent written scores before discussion, a decision rule other than a single veto); respects candidates' time and personal information; handles a teammate's round with data and respect; measures success by consistency, pass rates by round, acceptance and later performance, not just volume; brings the team along; real example with own actions, measures and lessons, or honestly hypothetical; never presents any company's actual hiring process as the model.

clarifications.q: Are the rounds written down?
clarifications.a: Each interviewer has their own questions; there is a one-line description per round.

clarifications.q: Is there a scoring rubric?
clarifications.a: Interviewers write free-text feedback and a hire or no-hire vote.

clarifications.q: Who makes the decision?
clarifications.a: A debrief of the interviewers, where any single strong no usually ends it.

clarifications.q: Do you have data on past candidates?
clarifications.a: Stage outcomes, votes and dates for the last 18 months.

hints: Look at pass rates per round and per interviewer before touching any question; a funnel shows where good candidates are lost.
Ask what each round is meant to measure, and whether that is something the job needs.
You rarely learn about false negatives directly; look for the signals you do have and treat them as samples, not proof.
followups: What would you look at first in the 18 months of outcomes and votes, and what would worry you?
How do you make the rounds measure what the job needs, and the scoring consistent between interviewers?
A respected teammate's round rejects far more candidates than the others, and they say it protects the bar. How do you handle it?
How would you know in {{months}} months whether the process is better without simply hiring more people?
In your real example, what changed in how people were assessed, and how did you measure it?

rules.ask: Your manager said not to lower the bar. How is what you propose different, and how would you show it?
Who writes the rubric, how do you check two interviewers score the same answer the same way, and how often?
How long does it really take candidates, and who drops out because of it?
What exactly would that round measure, and how would two interviewers agree on it?
What would you measure in the outcomes to see whether the process treats different groups of candidates differently?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for an open hub of models, datasets and apps
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, scaling onto an open hub

angle: the bottleneck that was hardest to find
the decision that most changed what the system cost
the failure that taught you the most
hub_feature: anyone can publish, so inputs are untrusted and their sizes unbounded
every revision is kept in git history, so nothing published is ever simply overwritten
a few repositories take most of the traffic, and one new release can take a large share of it within an hour

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or users depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change if it ran inside, or served, an open hub of models, datasets and apps at {{scale}} today's load, where {{hub_feature}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes at {{scale}} the load on an open hub where {{hub_feature}}. If you have never worked on a public platform with user-published content, say so, pick the closest system you have worked on, and be clear which parts you are recalling and which you are reasoning through.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The open-hub setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers (volume, peak and average, latency or throughput targets, cost); depth on the chosen angle down to data paths, bottlenecks and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; an honest account of what broke and what changed; a scaling analysis that names the first bottleneck and how it would be seen early; concrete reasoning about the hub feature (limits and isolation for untrusted input, storage and deletion when history is kept, hot-item handling and cache warm-up for uneven popularity) with its new failure modes; own contribution separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to involve machine learning?
clarifications.a: No. Any system that moves, stores or computes data others depend on counts; the hub part is reasoning.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to data paths, bottlenecks, failure modes, costs and numbers.

clarifications.q: What is special about an open hub for this question?
clarifications.a: Content comes from anyone, is versioned, and its popularity is extremely uneven. Reason from those.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers, including peak against average, before the architecture.
Know where the time and money go in your system, and which input would hurt it most if someone you do not trust supplied it.
For the hub question, ask what happens when one item suddenly takes most of the traffic, and what happens when nothing can be overwritten.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
At {{scale}} the load, which component fails first, and how would you know before users did?
How would your system cope when {{hub_feature}}, and what new failure does that bring?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
One new release takes a large share of all traffic within an hour. What does your cache do in the first minute, before it is warm?
Someone uploads a file a thousand times larger than anything you tested. Which part of your system notices first, and what does it do?
How did you prove that was the bottleneck rather than a symptom of something upstream?
What did the system cost per month, which part drove it, and what did you change because of it?
